terms.short: How your money is split between equity, debt, gold and cash
terms.definition: How a portfolio is divided between asset classes such as shares, bonds or debt funds, gold and cash. It drives most of a portfolio's long-run return and most of its ups and downs, more than which individual stocks or funds you pick. The right split depends on when you need the money and how much of a fall you can live with.
examples: With a 70:30 equity-debt split, a 30% market crash cuts the portfolio by about 21%, not 30%.

terms.short: Bringing your mix back to its target
terms.definition: Selling some of what has grown beyond its target share and adding to what has shrunk, so the portfolio returns to its chosen asset allocation. It keeps risk from creeping up after a long rally and makes you trim what has risen and add to what has fallen. People usually do it once a year or when the mix drifts by more than a few percentage points; selling can trigger capital gains tax.
examples: After a strong year, equity was 80% of her portfolio against a 70% target, so she moved the extra 10% into debt.

terms.short: How long until you need the money
terms.definition: How long the money can stay invested before you need it. Equity can fall sharply in any one year but has usually recovered over longer periods, so it suits goals five or more years away; money needed within a year or two is usually kept in debt funds or deposits, where it won't fall much just when you need it.
examples: The house down payment is due in 18 months, so that money shouldn't be in small-cap funds.

terms.short: How much of a fall you can live with
terms.definition: How large a temporary loss an investor can sit through without selling in panic or needing the money. It depends on income, savings, goals and temperament. A useful test: imagine the portfolio down 30% in a year, as happened in 2008 and early 2020, and ask what you would do.
examples: He sold everything in the March 2020 crash, which showed his real risk tolerance was lower than his questionnaire said.

terms.definition: A share in a large, long-established company with a strong position and a record of steady profits, usually part of indices like the Nifty 50 or Sensex. Blue chips tend to be less volatile than smaller companies, but they can still fall a lot, and a famous name says nothing about whether the share price is good value.
examples: Even blue chips fell 30% in the March 2020 crash.

terms.short: Company expected to grow profits fast, usually priced high
terms.definition: A share in a company whose sales and profits are expected to grow much faster than the market's. Investors pay a high price-to-earnings multiple for that growth, so the price can fall hard if growth slows even a little, or when interest rates rise. Growth investing means buying such companies and holding them while the growth lasts.
examples: The stock trades at 70 times earnings, so the market expects years of fast growth.

terms.short: Share that looks cheap against its profits or assets
terms.definition: A share that trades at a low price compared with its earnings, book value or cash flow, often because the company is out of favour or growing slowly. Value investing means buying such shares expecting the price to catch up with what the business is worth. The risk is a value trap: a share that is cheap because the business is getting worse.
examples: The PSU bank traded at 0.6 times book value, which value investors saw as cheap.

terms.short: Lasting edge that keeps competitors away
terms.definition: A lasting advantage that lets a company keep earning high returns because rivals can't easily copy it: a strong brand, a large network of users, low costs from scale, high costs for customers to switch, patents or licences. Companies with wide moats tend to show a high return on capital that stays high for many years.
examples: Its distribution reach in rural India is a moat that new brands take a decade to match.

terms.short: Very cheap, very small share: high risk
terms.definition: A share trading at a very low price, often a few rupees, in a very small company. A low price does not mean cheap: what matters is the price compared with earnings and assets. Penny stocks are often illiquid, thinly researched and a favourite target of pump-and-dump schemes and stock tips on social media.
examples: The ₹3 stock doubled on a Telegram tip, then hit the lower circuit for a week.

terms.short: Stock that has risen many times over
terms.definition: A stock whose price has risen several times over, such as a 'ten-bagger' that went up tenfold. The word is usually used looking back. Lists of 'future multibaggers' are guesses, and for every share that multiplies many others fall or stagnate.
examples: A ₹10,000 investment that became ₹1 lakh made it a ten-bagger.

terms.short: Share bought mainly for regular dividends
terms.definition: A share in a company that pays out a large part of its profits as dividends every year, often a mature business with steady cash flow, such as many public sector companies, utilities and FMCG firms. A very high dividend yield can be a warning sign: it may mean the price has fallen because investors expect profits, and the dividend, to drop.
examples: The PSU's 7% dividend yield looked attractive until it cut the payout the next year.

terms.short: Government bond linked to the gold price
terms.definition: A bond issued by the RBI on behalf of the government whose value follows the price of gold, paying 2.5% a year interest on the original amount on top. It runs for eight years, and gains are tax-free if held to maturity. The government has not issued new tranches since early 2024; existing bonds trade on the stock exchanges, often at a discount or premium to the gold price.
examples: SGBs bought in 2016 were redeemed in 2024 at more than double their issue price, plus eight years of interest.
terms.note: Check the RBI's current notices before relying on the details: redemption prices and any new issues are announced there.

terms.short: Exchange-traded fund that holds physical gold
terms.definition: An exchange-traded fund that holds physical gold and whose units track the gold price, bought and sold on the exchange through a demat account. It avoids making charges, purity worries and storage, but charges a small yearly expense ratio. Gold funds (fund of funds) invest in gold ETFs for people without a demat account.
examples: She holds 10% of her portfolio in a gold ETF as a hedge against equity crashes and a weak rupee.

terms.short: Bank deposit at a fixed rate for a fixed time
terms.definition: Money placed with a bank or other lender for a fixed period at an interest rate fixed upfront. The capital doesn't move with markets, and bank deposits are insured by the DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank. Interest is taxed at your income-tax slab rate every year, so the after-tax return is often close to inflation.
examples: A 7% FD taxed at 30% gives about 4.9% after tax, barely above inflation.
